"Shaiking" it up (Foetal Surgery in SA)

By: Julie Laurenz | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It has been two years since we watched baby Ford being born after lifesaving in utero surgery. Sadly many parents aren’t aware of or have access to these procedures. One SA doctor hopes to change th

Summary:
SUMMARY
We first met Dr Samad Shaik in July 2012, when he successfully operated on Joel Ford,
then a 32 week old foetus who had developed an extremely rare medical condition called
chylothorax. Fluid had filled his chest cavity compressing the lungs and displacing the heart. Neither organ was able to grow properly and there was a chance the pressure would stop the heart from beating.

Dr Shaik inserted a shunt that drained the fluid and two weeks later the little boy was born healthy. We were there. Today his dad “Hayden” describes Joel as a little “tiger” who celebrated his 2nd birthday in July this year.
DR SHAIKS VISION
But things could have been very different had their gynaecologist not introduced them to Dr Shaik – one of only a handful of foetal surgeons in the country. (He says he is the only Paediatric Surgeon in the country who has been performing some of these major surgeries. EXIT procedures without major surgery on placental support are being done in some hospitals – like the Nel case below.)
According to Dr Shaik, many parents are advised to terminate pregnancies when potentially fatal conditions are detected in the womb. (He says this is especially true in the Cape). It’s a situation he hopes to change. He says many babies can be saved.
He is advocating for the creation of at least two foetal surgery units to be established in Cape Town and possibly Johannesburg.
Significantly he wants these units to be available to be set up at state hospitals, where ordinary South Africans can have access to this specialise surgery AND where young surgeons can be trained in the discipline.
He hopes to be able to offer desperate parents a whole bunch of lifesaving procedures.


Further information:
VITAL SERVICE
Hospitals in South Africa are beginning to see Foetal Surgery as a vital service they can offer to their patients.
In August a medical team at Mediclinic performed what’s called an “Exit Procedure” on a baby Nel. The baby was diagnosed with a massive growth on his neck.

It’s called an “ex uteror intrapartum treatment “This is where the baby is partially delivered and then whilst still connected to the placenta and the mother, an operation is performed on the baby. The child remains on placental bypass and therefore the mother takes care of all baby’s needs whilst the surgery is being performed.
The clinic recorded interviews with both parents and the surgeon. BUT unfortunately it was done in progressive on a 5D. So we will have to reshoot the interview ourselves...which is best anyway!
NB: We have footage from inside the operating theatre. It’s a gopro shot from directly above. You can see the baby’s head sticking out and the surgery being done. The baby is then delivered.
The mom speaks about how the whole town was behind them. I think to would really add to the story to go Calvinia. (4hrs from CT. Maybe I go alone without a presenter?). The whole small town thing is sweet and I think we need to meet the baby.
We would also interview their surgeon about the value of these surgeries and how more surgeons capable of these surgeries are needed.
GROWING THE SKILLS

According to Dr Shaik the procedures done on Baby Ford and Nel are just the start. In the past few years he has been pioneering and perfecting a variety of treatments that can be done on babies still in utro.
NB: Dr Shaik has video recordings of all his surgeries which we can use and he is arranging for us to talk to some of the families.
• The Laybrand Twins

A year ago he did Foetoscopy and LASER ablation for twin to twin transfusion syndrome (TTTTS) .
This is a cruel disease where a set of twins are connected to each other by abnormal blood vessels in the placenta. One twin then “steals” all the blood from the other twin resulting in one that is overloaded with fluid and growing quickly but the heart is unable to cope and the other twin (donor), becomes smaller and smaller as its blood is drained.
He inserted a tiny telescope into the womb and used a LASER to “disconnect” or interrupt these connections and resolve the problem. Untreated both twins would die. Unfortunately the family had been referred too late and one twin died. But without treatment both would certainly have perished.
He says he will find us at least one other case to illustrate one of the other types of surgeries he’s been doing:

Vesico amniotic shunts – insertion of a special catheter into the bladder of a baby when there is obstruction to the baby’s bladder outlet. The foetus can therefore not pass urine, mom has less fluid, baby develops poorly, kidneys are damaged and the lungs develop poorly. Additionally the kidneys are damaged due to the obstruction and kidney failure often results. The catheter is inserted and bypasses the obstruction.
Resection of pulmonary sequestration – in some children, part of the lung develops abnormally and grows like a tumour to displace the small bit of remaining normal lung. This can cause many problems including “stealing the blood” from the rest of the body and thus the heart has to work harder resulting in a form of heart failure. In a small group of patients this lump has to be removed or the blood supply to it interrupted before baby is born to ensure survival. So far we have had one child that has needed this.
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) – here, there is a hole in the diaphragm and the intestines move into the chest cavity. This results in compression of the lungs and heart. It is often a fatal condition. We have used several different options for this condition – perform a bronchoscopy (pass a special telescope through the uterus, through baby’s mouth and into the trachea and then place a balloon in it to block the trachea and allow the lungs to grow till delivery; repair the CDH just before baby is delivered whilst still on placental support (OOPS – operation on placental support).
Gastroschisis – in this condition the bowel all lies outside the abdomen through a hole in the wall of the abdomen. These babies are delivered and surgery is performed immediately to return the bowel into the abdomen.
SPINA BIFIDA
This is where Dr Shaik hopes to make a significant difference. He says Spina Bifida repairs can also be done. It’s a common procedure in USA, but not here. The surgery improves quality of life significantly.
He says Foetal surgery is a rapidly changing field and new procedures are being regularly explored – its time South Africa got up to speed.
Currently Dr Shaik is at the Tygerberg Hospital on “sabbatical”. He says he’s there to consult with the academics in order to bring his vision to fruition.
PLAN:
I could interview the Durban Cases on my own.
Presenter: The Nel Case/Dr Shaik and the surgeon who performed the Nel Exit procedure. All in the Cape.

Script:


FEOTAL SURGERY “SHAIKING IT UP”

Joel Ford is a happy and healthy little boy. And keeps his parents - Hayden and Tarryn Ford on their toes.

Tarryn: He is a little ball of energy. Ja, he’s wonderful.
Hayden: 100% go all the time.

Sound UP: “Daddy daddy”

It’s hard to believe that two years ago, little Joel’s life had been (“was?” not sure on grammar here) in serious danger... before he’d even been born.

When Taryyn was 5 months pregnant, a routine scan showed that Joel had an extremely rare medical condition called chylothorax.

Blocked Lymphatic ducts in the chest had caused fluid to leak into the torso, compressing the
lungs and displacing the heart. There was a strong possibility that his heart would stop beating.


But thanks to remarkable surgery performed on the unborn foetus while it is in the uterus by a team of Durban doctors lead by Professor Samad Shaik, this baby fought incredible odds and won.

When he was finally delivered at 34 weeks, the shunt was clamped ... and removed.

Devi: How are you feeling?
Professor Bhorat:
We are all shaking!
(Laugh)

Tarryn owes her son’s life to Professor Shaik and his team.

Tarryn: We were very fortunate to have had him in our lives, and continue to have him in our lives and I hope that other people get that same opportunity.

Professor Shaik says Joel’s surgery was a game changer.

Professor Shaik: What that seemed to allow was the entire Foetal Interventions to snow
ball ... to a number of patients actually being referred or requesting an assessment.

Joel Ford’s was the first in-utero procedure done by a foetal surgeon in South Africa.

Professor Shaik and his team have done 19 more of these surgeries since.

LINK: Foetal intervention and surgery offers parents an alternative... there is a chance that
something can be done...and baby can be allowed to recuperate in the best intensive care
unit in the world...that of course is the mother’s womb.

John: Before Baby Ford what was the general response of the medical fraternity to
problems discovered in the womb?

Professor Shaik: The parents were offered three options. They could either continue with the
pregnancy and baby could either die or be delivered, and if the baby could be delivered could
be managed at that time, or, they could have a termination of pregnancy.

It is heartbreaking for parents to choose between these options - especially when there are two little lives at risk.

Gershon and Hailey Muller from Pinetown were 5 month pregnant with twins in July 2012 when their
gynaecologist broke the news that their babies had twin to twin transfusion syndrome.

LINK: This is a particularly cruel disease twins are connected to each other through abnormal blood vessels in the placenta. One twin then “steals” all the blood from the other, meaning that one becomes overloaded with fluid, while the other is starved of all its blood.


Hailey: He said that the gap was very big and if we don’t do anything you are going to loose them
both, or you could try something. And that something was an operation done by Doctor Shaik.

Professor Shaik recorded this extraordinary footage of the laser surgery he performed on Hailey’s
twins while in the womb.

John: It’s a very detailed picture isn’t it?
Professor Shaik: The actual telescope itself is 1.9mm in diameter and the picture is magnified
about 7 times.

With only this pinhole view inside the womb to guide the surgery, he began to close off blood
vessels that crisscross the placenta using a laser.

Professor Shaik: It’s almost like doing soldering, or welding. // So you disconnect one set of blood
vessels from the other child’s blood vessels and then make sure each baby has their own blood
supply and are not sharing the blood with each other.

John: Extraordinary!

Unfortunately the bigger of the two babies didn’t survive. His heart gave in a few weeks later.
Hailey was worried she’d also lose the smaller baby, who they had named Jaydon.

Hailey: And then some strange miracle by God grace, Jaydon started picking up his weight. He’s got
the fluid around him. Everything just started picking up and there was hope again. Jaydon could
actually make it.

Incredibly the tiniest twin was born healthy.

Gershon : The first thing the doctors said was, this baby does not need oxygen and as small as he
was, // I couldn’t, my legs were shaking and I was the most proud father in the world.

Jayden turned two in October.

Despite these success stories, Professor Shaik says South Africa is lagging behind other countries in
this field - because there is a lack of expertise. His dream is to set up specialised foetal surgical units
in country.

LINK: Significantly he wants to set up these units at state hospitals, so that ordinary South Africans ordinary South Africans can have access to this specialise surgery, and where young surgeons can be trained in the discipline.

Around 4% of children are born with abnormalities that could be dealt with while they are still in the womb.

Professor Shaik: Interestingly from a cost point of view it is not any more expensive than any other
surgical procedure that we would do. It can actually significantly reduce costs in the post natal
period.

These units will offer desperate parents a range of life saving interventions.

One of these is the Exit surgery performed on Baby Ruben Nel by a team of doctors from Mediclinic in
Cape Town in August last year.

LINK: It’s called an “ex uteror intrapartum treatment “This is where the baby is partially delivered and then whilst still connected to the placenta and the mother, an operation is performed on the baby.

Ronelle and Johan Nel live in Calvina, a small farming town north of Cape Town.

Ronelle was pregnant with the couple’s third child ...and 22 weeks along, when a scan revealed a growth on the baby’s neck.

Johan: It’s not nice, hey! It’s a big shock.

Ronelle: It took me ten minutes and I just started sobbing and that whole day was shock, I
was in shock the whole day.

A massive cyst was blocking Baby Ruben’s trachea. The only way to ensure he survived birth would be
to partially deliver him to open the airway and then cut the umbilical cord - which was until then
Ruben’s source of oxygen from the placenta.

But it was too early in the pregnancy to go ahead with the surgery – so it became a waiting game.

John: It must have been excruciating.
Ronelle: Ja, it was terrible. // I couldn’t afford to fall apart because I had two other
children that needed a mother and ... so that was very hard for me. As well as my
baby that was growing inside of me.// It was quite difficult to stay positive without positive
news.

10 long weeks passed before the surgery was given the green light.

Paediatrician Dr Richard Alexander was in charge of intubating the baby.

Dr Alexander: And if I couldn’t intubate the baby and create an airway, then we would then go on
to the next discipline, the paediatric pulmonologist... and if he wasn’t able to establish an airway
with an endoscope and then the next speciality would have been an ears nose and throat surgeon
would have had to perform a tracheotomy.

Nothing was left to chance. At the most critical point there were at least 20 specialists in the
operating theatre.

At first Dr Alexander battled... But happily he was eventually able to get the oxygen tube down
Rubens constricted airway.

UPSOUND : They all cheer

And with Ruben able to breathe, the umbilical chord was cut.

Johan: After all those weeks of wondering.Yes, dit is wonderlik.

Ruben was allowed to recuperate for a few days before the cyst was finally removed.

He has now fully recovered and is thriving.

Ronelle: I think if someone would have told me the year before that we would go through a year
like this, I would have thought that I would never make it. But we did and we made it. One is
stronger than one thinks.

Dr Alexander says there is a need for more foetal surgery units.

Dr Alexander: There needs to be certain centres where these babies are referred to where there has
been experience in dealing with such babies.

In utero procedures are regularly being developed and perfected.

Professor Shaik recently removed a tumor from the inside of a baby’s lung using an exit technique.

Only this time the baby stayed connected to the umbilical cord during the removal of the mass and
received the same anaesthetic given to the mother , via the placenta.

Professor Shaik: So mum does all the work and basically baby is held on life support, like a cardiac
by-pass machine on life support and that provides us with an extremely stable, well baby that we
can operate on without having to rush.

A telescope was then inserted into the baby’s chest and the lung tissue removed.

Professor Shaik: He went home a few days – about a week later perfectly well requiring
minimal treatment.

The only indication that the baby had had surgery was a small cut under his arm.

So far in procedures carried out locally, once a womb is open babies are delivered as soon as surgery
is completed.

But Professor Shaik says the next step is to operate and put the baby back into the
womb so that it can be delivered later at the right time – which is happening internationally.

John: It must be very rewarding.
Professor Shaik: One of the hospital groups where most of the surgery is performed organised a
reunion and we had about five children who had all undergone foetal surgery, from ages 2 to
about 4 months was the youngest child. And seeing them all in one situation was very gratifying.

Hailey: If Doctor Shaik’s plans is to have more foetal surgery units available to all it would be the
most awesome thing we could ever have in South Africa.

John: Extraordinary! Unfortunately the bigger of the two babies didn’t survive. His heart gave in a few weeks later. Hailey was worried she’d also lose the smaller baby, who they had named Jaydon. Hailey: And then some strange miracle by God grace, Jaydon started picking up his weight. He’s got the fluid around him. Everything just started picking up and there was hope again. Jaydon could actually make it. Incredibly the tiniest twin was born healthy. Gershon : The first thing the doctors said was, this baby does not need oxygen and as small as he was, // I couldn’t, my legs were shaking and I was the most proud father in the world. Jayden turned two in October. Despite these success stories, Professor Shaik says South Africa is lagging behind other countries in this field - because there is a lack of expertise. His dream is to set up specialised foetal surgical units in country. LINK: Significantly he wants to set up these units at state hospitals, so that ordinary South Africans ordinary South Africans can have access to this specialise surgery, and where young surgeons can be trained in the discipline. Around 4% of children are born with abnormalities that could be dealt with while they are still in the womb. Professor Shaik: Interestingly from a cost point of view it is not any more expensive than any other surgical procedure that we would do. It can actually significantly reduce costs in the post natal period. These units will offer desperate parents a range of life saving interventions. One of these is the Exit surgery performed on Baby Ruben Nel by a team of doctors from Mediclinic in Cape Town in August last year. LINK: It’s called an “ex uteror intrapartum treatment “This is where the baby is partially delivered and then whilst still connected to the placenta and the mother, an operation is performed on the baby. Ronelle and Johan Nel live in Calvina, a small farming town north of Cape Town. Ronelle was pregnant with the couple’s third child ...and 22 weeks along, when a scan revealed a growth on the baby’s neck. Johan: It’s not nice, hey! It’s a big shock. Ronelle: It took me ten minutes and I just started sobbing and that whole day was shock, I was in shock the whole day. A massive cyst was blocking Baby Ruben’s trachea. The only way to ensure he survived birth would be to partially deliver him to open the airway and then cut the umbilical cord - which was until then Ruben’s source of oxygen from the placenta. But it was too early in the pregnancy to go ahead with the surgery – so it became a waiting game. John: It must have been excruciating. Ronelle: Ja, it was terrible. // I couldn’t afford to fall apart because I had two other children that needed a mother and ... so that was very hard for me. As well as my baby that was growing inside of me.// It was quite difficult to stay positive without positive news. 10 long weeks passed before the surgery was given the green light. Paediatrician Dr Richard Alexander was in charge of intubating the baby. Dr Alexander: And if I couldn’t intubate the baby and create an airway, then we would then go on to the next discipline, the paediatric pulmonologist... and if he wasn’t able to establish an airway with an endoscope and then the next speciality would have been an ears nose and throat surgeon would have had to perform a tracheotomy. Nothing was left to chance. At the most critical point there were at least 20 specialists in the operating theatre. At first Dr Alexander battled... But happily he was eventually able to get the oxygen tube down Rubens constricted airway. UPSOUND : They all cheer And with Ruben able to breathe, the umbilical chord was cut. Johan: After all those weeks of wondering.Yes, dit is wonderlik. Ruben was allowed to recuperate for a few days before the cyst was finally removed. He has now fully recovered and is thriving. Ronelle: I think if someone would have told me the year before that we would go through a year like this, I would have thought that I would never make it. But we did and we made it. One is stronger than one thinks. Dr Alexander says there is a need for more foetal surgery units. Dr Alexander: There needs to be certain centres where these babies are referred to where there has been experience in dealing with such babies. In utero procedures are regularly being developed and perfected. Professor Shaik recently removed a tumor from the inside of a baby’s lung using an exit technique. Only this time the baby stayed connected to the umbilical cord during the removal of the mass and received the same anaesthetic given to the mother , via the placenta. Professor Shaik: So mum does all the work and basically baby is held on life support, like a cardiac by-pass machine on life support and that provides us with an extremely stable, well baby that we can operate on without having to rush. A telescope was then inserted into the baby’s chest and the lung tissue removed. Professor Shaik: He went home a few days – about a week later perfectly well requiring minimal treatment. The only indication that the baby had had surgery was a small cut under his arm. So far in procedures carried out locally, once a womb is open babies are delivered as soon as surgery is completed. But Professor Shaik says the next step is to operate and put the baby back into the womb so that it can be delivered later at the right time – which is happening internationally. John: It must be very rewarding. Professor Shaik: One of the hospital groups where most of the surgery is performed organised a reunion and we had about five children who had all undergone foetal surgery, from ages 2 to about 4 months was the youngest child. And seeing them all in one situation was very gratifying. Hailey: If Doctor Shaik’s plans is to have more foetal surgery units available to all it would be the most awesome thing we could ever have in South Africa. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): It has been two years since we watched baby Ford being born after lifesaving in utero surgery. Sadly many parents aren’t aware of or have access to these procedures. One SA doctor hopes to change th
metadata.Summary: SUMMARY We first met Dr Samad Shaik in July 2012, when he successfully operated on Joel Ford, then a 32 week old foetus who had developed an extremely rare medical condition called chylothorax. Fluid had filled his chest cavity compressing the lungs and displacing the heart. Neither organ was able to grow properly and there was a chance the pressure would stop the heart from beating. Dr Shaik inserted a shunt that drained the fluid and two weeks later the little boy was born healthy. We were there. Today his dad “Hayden” describes Joel as a little “tiger” who celebrated his 2nd birthday in July this year. DR SHAIKS VISION But things could have been very different had their gynaecologist not introduced them to Dr Shaik – one of only a handful of foetal surgeons in the country. (He says he is the only Paediatric Surgeon in the country who has been performing some of these major surgeries. EXIT procedures without major surgery on placental support are being done in some hospitals – like the Nel case below.) According to Dr Shaik, many parents are advised to terminate pregnancies when potentially fatal conditions are detected in the womb. (He says this is especially true in the Cape). It’s a situation he hopes to change. He says many babies can be saved. He is advocating for the creation of at least two foetal surgery units to be established in Cape Town and possibly Johannesburg. Significantly he wants these units to be available to be set up at state hospitals, where ordinary South Africans can have access to this specialise surgery AND where young surgeons can be trained in the discipline. He hopes to be able to offer desperate parents a whole bunch of lifesaving procedures.
metadata.Further information: VITAL SERVICE Hospitals in South Africa are beginning to see Foetal Surgery as a vital service they can offer to their patients. In August a medical team at Mediclinic performed what’s called an “Exit Procedure” on a baby Nel. The baby was diagnosed with a massive growth on his neck. It’s called an “ex uteror intrapartum treatment “This is where the baby is partially delivered and then whilst still connected to the placenta and the mother, an operation is performed on the baby. The child remains on placental bypass and therefore the mother takes care of all baby’s needs whilst the surgery is being performed. The clinic recorded interviews with both parents and the surgeon. BUT unfortunately it was done in progressive on a 5D. So we will have to reshoot the interview ourselves...which is best anyway! NB: We have footage from inside the operating theatre. It’s a gopro shot from directly above. You can see the baby’s head sticking out and the surgery being done. The baby is then delivered. The mom speaks about how the whole town was behind them. I think to would really add to the story to go Calvinia. (4hrs from CT. Maybe I go alone without a presenter?). The whole small town thing is sweet and I think we need to meet the baby. We would also interview their surgeon about the value of these surgeries and how more surgeons capable of these surgeries are needed. GROWING THE SKILLS According to Dr Shaik the procedures done on Baby Ford and Nel are just the start. In the past few years he has been pioneering and perfecting a variety of treatments that can be done on babies still in utro. NB: Dr Shaik has video recordings of all his surgeries which we can use and he is arranging for us to talk to some of the families. • The Laybrand Twins A year ago he did Foetoscopy and LASER ablation for twin to twin transfusion syndrome (TTTTS) . This is a cruel disease where a set of twins are connected to each other by abnormal blood vessels in the placenta. One twin then “steals” all the blood from the other twin resulting in one that is overloaded with fluid and growing quickly but the heart is unable to cope and the other twin (donor), becomes smaller and smaller as its blood is drained. He inserted a tiny telescope into the womb and used a LASER to “disconnect” or interrupt these connections and resolve the problem. Untreated both twins would die. Unfortunately the family had been referred too late and one twin died. But without treatment both would certainly have perished. He says he will find us at least one other case to illustrate one of the other types of surgeries he’s been doing: Vesico amniotic shunts – insertion of a special catheter into the bladder of a baby when there is obstruction to the baby’s bladder outlet. The foetus can therefore not pass urine, mom has less fluid, baby develops poorly, kidneys are damaged and the lungs develop poorly. Additionally the kidneys are damaged due to the obstruction and kidney failure often results. The catheter is inserted and bypasses the obstruction. Resection of pulmonary sequestration – in some children, part of the lung develops abnormally and grows like a tumour to displace the small bit of remaining normal lung. This can cause many problems including “stealing the blood” from the rest of the body and thus the heart has to work harder resulting in a form of heart failure. In a small group of patients this lump has to be removed or the blood supply to it interrupted before baby is born to ensure survival. So far we have had one child that has needed this. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) – here, there is a hole in the diaphragm and the intestines move into the chest cavity. This results in compression of the lungs and heart. It is often a fatal condition. We have used several different options for this condition – perform a bronchoscopy (pass a special telescope through the uterus, through baby’s mouth and into the trachea and then place a balloon in it to block the trachea and allow the lungs to grow till delivery; repair the CDH just before baby is delivered whilst still on placental support (OOPS – operation on placental support). Gastroschisis – in this condition the bowel all lies outside the abdomen through a hole in the wall of the abdomen. These babies are delivered and surgery is performed immediately to return the bowel into the abdomen. SPINA BIFIDA This is where Dr Shaik hopes to make a significant difference. He says Spina Bifida repairs can also be done. It’s a common procedure in USA, but not here. The surgery improves quality of life significantly. He says Foetal surgery is a rapidly changing field and new procedures are being regularly explored – its time South Africa got up to speed. Currently Dr Shaik is at the Tygerberg Hospital on “sabbatical”. He says he’s there to consult with the academics in order to bring his vision to fruition. PLAN: I could interview the Durban Cases on my own. Presenter: The Nel Case/Dr Shaik and the surgeon who performed the Nel Exit procedure. All in the Cape.
